transcript:
[00:00] Sara Kim: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. we've got about an hour, i'll hand off to victor for the runtime sections and then we'll dig into networking.
[00:08] Victor Chen: cool, thanks sara. hi acme team. quick context — you've been evaluating private deployments to keep PHI in your VPC and avoid public egress. we want to cover both networking and the runtime tradeoffs.
[00:22] Liam Patel: yep, that's right. main ask from execs is: can we run inference without any internet egress, maintain sub 150ms p95 latency for our chat endpoints, and keep costs predictable.
[00:35] Maria Gomez: and we have strict egress budgeting; NAT gateway costs spike with sustained outbound traffic.
[00:42] Victor Chen: ok good. quick high-level: for Private VPC we offer PrivateLink endpoints + VPC endpoints that let you keep traffic inside aws backbone. alternative is VPC peering or Transit Gateway — each has different routing and cross-account rules. PrivateLink gives you endpoint ENIs in your subnet, good for stable private DNS names.
[00:59] Noah Reed: how does that work with our DNS? we run conditional forwarding for internal zones.
[01:05] Victor Chen: Private DNS can be auto-enabled so the redwood-hosted private endpoint resolves to the ENI IPs. if you do conditional forwarders, you need to ensure the resolver can reach the AWS VPC resolver. sometimes teams add a Route 53 resolver inbound endpoint.
[01:20] Sara Kim: right — and note we can support both PrivateLink and Transit Gateway; Transit is better at scale for many VPCs but cost differs.
[01:28] Liam Patel: cost vs latency tradeoff — will PrivateLink add latency?
[01:33] Victor Chen: negligible, usually a few ms. the bigger sources of latency are serialization, network MTU mismatches, and cross-AZ hops if your inference fleet is in different AZs than the ENIs.
[01:44] Maria Gomez: okay, cross-AZ hairpinning — can you explain hairpinning? i get the NAT hairpin but for endpoints.
[01:50] Victor Chen: sure. hairpinning occurs if the request goes out from an AZ to a shared gateway and then back to a different AZ where the instance lives; that adds a 5–20ms hit typically. we recommend colocating endpoint ENIs and inference nodes in same AZs and using AZ-aware routing or placement groups when you run your fleet.
[02:08] Sara Kim: also, if you use VPC peering you can avoid some of that but peers are flat — scale and transitive routing is harder. Transit Gateway avoids peering scale issues.
[02:17] Liam Patel: about NAT and egress — if we keep everything private, do you ever need outbound egress?
[02:23] Victor Chen: you still need to pull model artifacts, container images, and sometimes reach KMS or key wrapping endpoints if keys are in cloud KMS. best practice: use S3 VPC endpoints for artifacts and a VPC endpoint for KMS or a proxy that sits in your control plane subnet. for KMS you can restrict via VPC endpoint policies.
[02:41] Noah Reed: our security team wants HSM-backed keys; do you integrate with customer KMS/HSM?
[02:46] Sara Kim: yes we support customer-managed keys; for Private deployments you can bring-your-own-KMS and we can integrate via endpoint. we'll send the integration guide.
[02:54] Victor Chen: switching to runtime: we talked about KV cache and batching. acme's workload is mixed — short chat sessions and some long-document summarization. KV cache helps for multi-turn chats by keeping decoder KV in memory, reducing compute per token.
[03:09] Liam Patel: what's the expected hit to latency when KV cache warms up?
[03:13] Victor Chen: on a warm cache, you often see 30–50% per-token compute reduction for multi-turn. absolute latency still depends on model size. for example, on a 70B float16 model with efficient kernels you might go from 180ms to 110ms p95 for short tokens when cache is hot.
[03:29] Maria Gomez: we saw a reference to quantization — is that safe for our health use-cases?
[03:34] Victor Chen: quantization (e.g., 4-bit or 8-bit) reduces memory / bandwidth and can reduce latency but may have small accuracy regressions. we recommend running evaluation suites on your prompts. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles per model and workload.
[03:50] Sara Kim: to add — our rollout tooling supports canarying quantized variants and automatic fallback to full-precision if quality drifts.
[03:58] Liam Patel: how about batching? we can't introduce tail latency for interactive chat.
[04:02] Victor Chen: we recommend dynamic batching with latency SLOs: small micro-batches for tail-sensitive routes and larger batches for throughput-y endpoints like embeddings. our runtime supports continuous batching and you can set max-latency thresholds per route. there's also per-customer shaping you can configure.
[04:19] Maria Gomez: do you have metrics around batching benefits? like tokens/sec improvement?
[04:23] Victor Chen: yes — batching can give 2–6x throughput improvements depending on model and beam size. tokens/sec improves because kernels are amortized; but packing sequences of varying lengths matters. we typically measure average tokens/sec and p95 latency across runs.
[04:37] Liam Patel: for the benchmark we want: 150ms p95 for chat at 200 concurrent users. is that realistic?
[04:44] Victor Chen: depends on model and hardware. for smaller open models on A10G-like infra it's challenging; on A100/H100 or optimized instances with quantized weights + KV cache we can often meet that. we'll propose a benchmark configuration.
[04:56] Sara Kim: operational note — when you run the benchmark in your VPC against our PrivateLink endpoint, watch for NAT gateway egress if your test harness still resolves external DNS. set up VPC endpoints for service control plane traffic to avoid unexpected egress.
[05:10] Noah Reed: about DNS — if we enable Private DNS, do we still need custom resolver entries?
[05:15] Victor Chen: Private DNS usually takes care of the *.redwood-inference.internal names. if you have on-prem resolvers or hybrid setups, you'll need inbound resolver endpoints or conditional forwarding so on-prem can resolve the private names.
[05:26] Maria Gomez: do you support mTLS between the inference nodes and our callers?
[05:30] Sara Kim: yes we support mutual TLS for client-to-endpoint traffic and you can layer additional network policies. for service-to-service we also support cert rotation via our control plane integration.
[05:38] Liam Patel: curious about observability — we need token-level costs and per-route latency traces. can that be exported into our Splunk?
[05:45] Victor Chen: absolutely. we can stream metrics to your observability backend via private collection agents or through an agent running in your VPC that pushes to your Splunk over HTTP(S). we'll share sample dashboards.
[05:57] Maria Gomez: slightly worried about cross-account IAM permissions for the endpoints. any gotchas?
[06:01] Victor Chen: ensure your endpoint policies only allow the required principals. we recommend least privilege: endpoint policy scoped to the Redwood service principal + IAM roles for the worker nodes. also consider using AWS Resource Access Manager for shared infra.
[06:16] Sara Kim: okay let's walk through a sample subnet layout: 3 private subnets (one per AZ) for inference nodes, a management subnet for control plane agents with outbound-only via NAT or proxy, and separate security group for the PrivateLink ENIs.
[06:33] Maria Gomez: what about IP exhaustion — ENIs per endpoint can eat addresses.
[06:37] Victor Chen: yes ENI density per subnet matters. we recommend /20-sized subnets for each AZ depending on expected scale; we'll provide a table with ENI consumption per connection.
[06:48] Liam Patel: can you summarize the recommended path for us?
[06:51] Sara Kim: recommended: use PrivateLink for a minimal-ops initial setup, colocate inference nodes in same AZs as ENIs to avoid hairpinning, enable Private DNS, use S3 and KMS endpoints to avoid egress, and run a benchmark with KV cache + dynamic batching. if you need multi-VPC scale use Transit Gateway and consider transit egress costs.
[07:12] Noah Reed: from a compliance lens, we need audit logs for model access and prompt content retention rules. how's that handled?
[07:19] Victor Chen: for Private we can ship audit logs into your account or a customer-managed S3 with lifecycle rules. we also support token-level redaction and configurable retention windows. will include details in the security packet.
[07:33] Maria Gomez: testing and rollout — how do we canary changes?
[07:36] Sara Kim: Redwood Console supports canaries by traffic split, A/B, and automatic rollback based on quality/regression alerts. you can bind routes to particular model versions (quantized or fp16) and hold back traffic until metrics pass.
[07:50] Liam Patel: ok great. one more — what about on-prem air-gapped installs? we might evaluate in a lab.
[07:57] Victor Chen: we offer an on-prem package; networking there is different: you run a control plane connector that talks to our control plane over an approved outbound during provisioning or via an RFC for offline bundles. we'll share the on-prem checklist.
[08:09] Sara Kim: time check — about 10 minutes left. any final technical clarifications?
[08:13] Maria Gomez: can you include the expected kernel and model optimizations (like flash attention builds) for our benchmark?
[08:18] Victor Chen: yes. our benchmark doc will list kernel versions, cuDNN/oneAPI variants, attention optimizations, quantization libs, and how we pack sequences for batching.
[08:27] Noah Reed: also include guidance on KMS key policies for cross-account use.
[08:30] Sara Kim: noted. we'll send the security pack.
[08:33] Liam Patel: recap and next steps?
[08:36] Sara Kim: recap: we'll send network diagram + PrivateLink vs Transit guidance, benchmark plan with scripts, security pack with KMS/HSM integration, and a proposed schedule for the lab run. maria will share VPC CIDRs and NAT counts. victor will prepare the benchmark. we'll target the week of 9/28 for the lab.
[08:53] Victor Chen: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with attachments and links to the docs referenced (network diagram pdf, benchmark repo, security pack).
[08:59] Liam Patel: thanks all. good session.
[09:02] Sara Kim: thanks — bye.
